newsitem.title: CHINA: Intel Corp sees big China computer market.
newsitem.headline: Intel Corp sees big China computer market.

text.p: China's personal computer buyers are as hungry for new technology as their Western counterparts and the Chinese market could be the world's second largest after the U.S. in under five years, a senior Intel Corp official said on Tuesday.

Intel's new range of Pentium processer chips had pushed aside older lines in 1996 as Chinese personal computer (PC) buyers leapfrogged to catch up with technology in the United States, said Intel Vice President Sean Maloney.
Personal computer sales were also rising far faster than more developed markets elsewhere, Maloney said in an interview.
"I would say that (China) will catch up with Japan as a market in the next three to four years," he said.
"Within the next five years it could be the world's second largest computer market," he said "It's a huge, huge market."
Official estimates put personal computer sales at 1.8 million in 1996.
The dramatic expansion of the Chinese market had been a factor in the growing importance to Intel of revenues generated in the Asia-Pacific region, he said.
Asia-Pacific excluding Japan had supplied 18 percent of total revenues in 1996, up from 14 percent in 1994, company figures showed.
"I think it will go above 20 percent," Maloney said, but declined to give details.
Intel was spending heavily on television advertising to build brand awareness in China, where progress had been made in curbing the remarking of its chips.

Intel had cooperated with Hong Kong and Chinese law enforcement agencies to crack down on pirate companies that ground off the top of chips and lasered on markings showing them as higher price models, Maloney said.
Growth in the number of service providers offering access to the Internet had provided a further boost to the personal computer market, he said.
"The last kind of roadblock to the PC taking off is gone," he said.

Intel's $99 million flash memory chip assembly and test plant near China's eastern city of Shanghai was expected to be on line before the end of February in 1998, said Jim Jarrett, president of Intel China.
The plant, in Shanghai's Pudong free trade zone, is the first phase of a $230 million chip fabrication plan, but no decision had been announced on a second stage, Jarrett said.
